turn_text: I think we need to remake the case for international trade. I think it was so apparent to most of us that we quit talking about it because so much prosperity had been created in the last many decades that people quit arguing about. In fact, it was one of the arguments in economics departments and universities that was largely won. I can remember saying 20 years ago, we don't have to argue about free trade anymore because people have decided and all the economics departments are basically arguing that free trade is a good thing. And now the rhetoric is the opposite, and to be fair, really both candidates, both Trump and Harris, are protectionists and advocating for more. To my mind, the constitutional position or libertarian constitutional position has always been that we divide up power and we constrain power. and we largely constrained power by dividing it up but it has constraints of the constitution so basically legislative actions are done by congress and the executive actions or uh... enforcing the law done by the executive the executive doesn't get to write law But over the last several decades, we've sort of given up on having trade policy decided by Congress. They said, it's too messy. Congress will never figure it out. It's easy for one president to negotiate with another president. So we kind of largely abdicated this role. And I'm very, very worried because I don't want any president, whether it's Biden or Harris, to have the power to invoke terrorists, because I think tariffs are bad. Now, the case for free trade is overwhelming. The average American consumer saves about $7,000 a year based on international trade. Even trade with the one adversary that everybody seems to be angry with right now, sometimes justifiably so, China About $1,500 is saved by every American because we trade with China. And so I think trade is without question a good thing and has enriched Americans as well as enriched those who are trading with us. But we've got to get back to talking about the benefits of that trade as opposed to somehow believing, oh, we're going to rejuvenate the steel industry. And it's gotten even beyond trade now. We have people so fearful of others or foreigners that they are not wanting even a Japanese company own a U.S. steel company anymore. So I think we've taken many steps backwards and frankly what Donald Trump's proposing won't work. What it will do will be raise prices. And the reason it works rhetorically and in politics is because if there's a steel factory, let's say in Cleveland and it employs a thousand people, those thousand people are very motivated and they see the benefit to them of tariffs. What we don't see is the unseen and that is the thousands of people across the United States who are actually buying that steel. whose prices will go up and then whose consumer goods will go up and the Americans will pay more and essentially the Americans will pay this tax. That's sort of the scene versus the unseen. And I believe that that's part of the problem with the argument. I think it's easy for politicians to make the argument for tariffs because you can see that bright, shiny factory that that person's wanting to protect. But what you're not seeing is that it's a net loss for the consumer and it's a net increase in prices for the consumer.
